visual.credit: Video: AP

beats.say: In France right now, teenagers are blockading their own schools.

sfx.prompt: distant street protest crowd and bins scraping on asphalt, outdoor

beats.say: With bins. With barriers. With human chains.

items.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: On October sixth, police counted about a quarter of a million people in the streets.

sfx.prompt: soft digital counter ticking, quiet clicks

beats.say: Organisers say it was four hundred and fifty thousand.
More than six thousand eight hundred people have been taken into police custody. Eighty-six percent of them are minors.

visual.name: blackfade
visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: One fifteen-year-old lost his hand.

sfx.prompt: single low sustained cello note, dark, quiet

beats.say: And it all started with a few empty classrooms, in one school outside Paris.
What are these teenagers so angry about?

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Why are so many of them ending up hurt, or in custody?
And can the government calm it down, before the next wave?

visual.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: deep low cinematic boom hit, soft, short dark tail

beats.say: This is what's happening in France's high schools, as of today.

visual.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: Créteil. A suburb just southeast of Paris.
Lycée Saint-Exupéry. About fifteen hundred pupils.
A lycée is a French high school, for fifteen- to eighteen-year-olds.
At the start of this school year, several teaching posts there were simply empty.
So in mid-September, the teachers went on strike.
The next day, the pupils joined in, their own way. They blocked the gates.
A few days later, two MPs from the radical-left party La France Insoumise visited, and posted about it.
Remember that visit. The government will.
Then, on September twenty-fourth, a rap-news outlet called Booska-P interviewed eight pupils from the school.
They talked about feeling abandoned, as kids from the banlieue, the working-class suburbs.
On TikTok, the clip was watched around one and a half million times.
And the idea spread with it. If your school is falling apart... block it.
By September twenty-fifth, around sixty schools in the Paris region were disrupted.
Three days later, the Interior Ministry counted one hundred and eighty, across France.
And on October first... one thousand and twenty-seven.
That's more than a quarter of all the lycées in France.
Teenagers don't shut down a thousand schools over one viral video.

visual.credit: Video: Reuters

beats.say: So what's actually going on inside these buildings?

visual.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: Let's walk inside a typical French lycée.
First, the building. On average, it's sixty-five years old.
More than half of France's lycées were built before 1970.
Pupils describe rats, cockroaches, and ceilings that have come down.
In summer, teachers report classrooms at thirty-five to forty degrees. In winter, some rooms have no heating at all.
A Senate report says fixing them would take about one and a half billion euros a year.
But for most pupils, the building isn't the biggest problem. It's who's missing from it.
This September, France's biggest secondary teachers' union surveyed over a thousand schools.
Fifty-three percent were missing at least one teacher.
The ministry disputes that. It says more than ninety-six percent of secondary posts are filled.
But by the ministry's own count, in 2024 to 2025, ten percent of lycée teaching hours simply didn't happen.
One pupil told Euronews they'd gone six months without a teacher, in an exam subject.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text.content: {\fs92}“Six months without a teacher,\Nin an exam subject.”\N{\fs50}{\c&HE6EEF2&}PUPIL, TO EURONEWS

beats.say: And when teachers are there, classrooms are packed. A teacher in Marseille says she has thirty-seven pupils in her class.
French lycée students also spend around twelve hundred hours a year in class. The average across OECD countries is nine hundred and sixty.
And at the end of all that, there's Parcoursup, the national platform that decides who gets into university.
This summer, eighteen percent of applicants got no offer at all in the main round. Two years ago, it was ten.

args.title: NO OFFER IN THE MAIN ROUND
args.source: Parcoursup data, via Le Monde, 11 Jul 2026

beats.say: Then, on October first, the government published its budget for 2027.
Education spending goes up, by about one point two billion euros.
But the same budget cuts one thousand five hundred and eighty-eight teaching posts.
The government points to about a hundred and eighty thousand fewer pupils expected.
The budget landed on the very day the protests hit their most violent point.
And that day, the map of France caught fire.

visual.credit: Procrastineur49, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: Here's how fast it moved.
First, the suburbs north and east of Paris. Saint-Denis. Sarcelles. La Courneuve.
Then Marseille. Lille. Lyon.
Then Nantes. Rennes. Bordeaux. Toulouse. Strasbourg.
On October first, the Interior Ministry counted one thousand nine hundred and forty-nine arrests. In a single day.
Two hundred and twenty-two lycées were fully blockaded.
In Nantes, a fire destroyed a lycée's entrance hall.
In Marseille, a firefighters' truck was torched, and the city shut down its entire bus and metro network.
The movement even crossed the border, into schools in Belgium, and then Italy.
On October second, prefects closed around four hundred lycées, and banned gatherings outside them.
The message from the state was clear. Stay home.
The pupils answered with a date. Tuesday, October sixth.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: In Paris, the march left Place de la République at two in the afternoon, heading for Nation.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: distant street protest crowd chanting, outdoor, muffled

beats.say: About two thousand police and gendarmes were deployed, with motorbike units and drones.

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Police counted fifty-six thousand people in Paris. Organisers said a hundred thousand.
In Lyon, twenty thousand, by police count. In Toulouse, thirteen and a half thousand.
And this time, it wasn't just the suburbs.

visual.credit: Video: AP

beats.say: Pupils from Louis-le-Grand and Henri-Quatre, two of the most elite schools in the country, walked out in solidarity.

visual.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: The placards said a lot.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: "Too young to be listened to, but not too young to be clubbed."

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text.content: {\fs92}“Too young to be listened to,\Nbut not too young to be clubbed.”\N{\fs50}{\c&HE6EEF2&}Trop jeune pour être écouté mais pas trop jeune pour être matraqué

beats.say: And in Perpignan, one banner read: "Sorry for the trouble. We just want a future."

visual.credit: Aurelio Cárdenas, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Across France: about a quarter of a million marchers, police say. Four hundred and fifty thousand, organisers say.
By evening, there was tear gas, at least four hundred and eighty-eight arrests, and forty-three officers wounded.

visual.credit: Video: Reuters

beats.say: Outside parliament, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a half-day in every lycée, for pupils to debate.

visual.credit: Video: AFP

beats.say: Headteachers' unions called it "a complete cacophony".

visual.credit: Wyslijp16, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Because by then, one question was dominating the news.
Why were teenagers getting hurt?

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: First, the tools.
French police use what they call "intermediate weapons".
The LBD, a launcher that fires rubber projectiles.
Launchers that fire tear-gas grenades.
And dispersal and stun grenades, which explode, some scattering rubber pellets.
On October second, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said there was no instruction to hold back. Officers could use all the intermediate weapons available.

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Then came three cases that changed the conversation.
September twenty-eighth. Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, northwest of Paris. A fourteen-year-old's jaw is broken by a tear-gas round, fired at close range.
Prosecutors say he had struck a policewoman first. On October sixth, the officer who fired was charged.
September thirtieth. Tours. A sixteen-year-old loses the use of an eye. The prosecutor says it's consistent with an LBD round.
October fifth. Lens, in the far north. A fifteen-year-old loses his hand to a police grenade.
A police source says he had picked it up to throw it back. The prosecutor says the shot followed procedure. His mother has filed a complaint.
Two days later, Nuñez suspended stun grenades at lycée protests, "until the facts are clarified".
The police watchdog, the IGPN, now has twenty-four investigations open.
Amnesty International, UNICEF France and the UN human rights office have all warned against disproportionate force.

visual.credit: Aurelio Cárdenas, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text.content: {\fs72}AMNESTY · UNICEF FRANCE · UN HUMAN RIGHTS OFFICE

beats.say: But the violence hasn't gone one way.
By the interior minister's count on October seventh, seven hundred and sixty-one police and gendarmes had been injured.
Along with two hundred and fifteen pupils, and eighty-nine school staff.
In Belfort, a plain-clothes police officer was beaten unconscious. Several minors have been charged.

visual.credit: Thomas Bresson, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Headteachers have been hit by fireworks.
No one has died.
So far, two thousand three hundred and seventy-six people have been prosecuted, most of them minors.

args.source: Justice Ministry, to 8 Oct 2026 (1,923 of them minors)

beats.say: So who does the government blame? And what is it actually offering?

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: Its first answer was political.

visual.credit: Video: LCP

beats.say: The prime minister's office called the movement an operation organised by La France Insoumise, and its allies on the far left.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text.content: {\fs92}“An operation organised by\NLa France Insoumise”\N{\fs50}{\c&HE6EEF2&}PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE, 1 OCT

beats.say: Remember those two MPs in Créteil?
But the newspaper Le Monde read the intelligence note behind that claim.
It covered one area, and a few days. It mentioned outsiders six times. The party, once.
The party denies organising anything, and accuses the government of conspiracy thinking.

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Lecornu has also said the voice of high-school students is precious, and must be heard.

text.content: {\fs92}“The voice of high-school students\Nis precious, and must be heard.”\N{\fs50}{\c&HE6EEF2&}SÉBASTIEN LECORNU, ON X

beats.say: Then came the offer. On October eighth, Education Minister Édouard Geffray went on prime-time TV.

visual.credit: Video: franceinfo

beats.say: Three thousand teachers, he said, would arrive within hours.
Three thousand and twenty-four supply teachers, already on the payroll, but not assigned to any classes.
They're going to the schools hit hardest: a hundred and fourteen "red" lycées, and about four hundred "orange" ones.
One pupil association called it a first concrete announcement.

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: Others weren't convinced. A seventeen-year-old in Nantes told France 24: "We don't want words. We want action."

text.content: {\fs92}“We don't want words.\NWe want action.”\N{\fs50}{\c&HE6EEF2&}PUPIL, 17, NANTES · FRANCE 24

beats.say: And critics asked the obvious question. If three thousand teachers were available, why weren't they in classrooms already?
Geffray admitted they hadn't been assigned.
Then there's the damage. Twenty-four lycées have been burned or ransacked.
About thirty thousand pupils have no classes in person.
Local officials say many of the fires were set by masked outsiders, not pupils.

visual.credit: Video: Reuters

beats.say: The government's estimate of the bill: at least thirty million euros.
So it's pushing a law nicknamed "casseurs-payeurs". Rioters pay.
Anyone in a group that causes damage could be made to pay up to ten thousand euros, even if they didn't break anything themselves.
And the public? In a poll for Le Figaro, sixty-two percent said the movement was justified.
But seventy-eight percent also said La France Insoumise was exploiting it.
So where does it go from here?

visual.credit: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sfx.prompt: soft low cinematic tone swell, gentle and quiet

beats.say: Right now, the blockades are shrinking.
On October first, more than a thousand lycées were affected. On October ninth, a hundred and forty-one were still closed.
A government source calls it a clear slowdown. Pupil unions say it's not over.
Here's the calendar.
Tuesday, October thirteenth. A national strike and day of action, called by student and teacher unions.
Saturday the seventeenth. A separate call that's been spreading on TikTok, from an anonymous account, about fuel prices, housing and discrimination.
It's not an official union date. But some lycée protesters have said they'll be there.
That same weekend, the autumn school holidays begin. Unions worry two weeks off could drain the movement.
October twenty-third. The government's online consultation for pupils closes.
October twenty-seventh. The rioters-pay bill goes to the Senate.
By the end of October, Lecornu has promised decisions, and changes to the budget.
And on November fifth, France's five biggest union confederations strike together, on pay and public services.
And behind all of it, a presidential election in April 2027.
In mid-September, this was about a few empty posts, at one school in Créteil.
Now, it's a question for the whole country.
What does France owe the teenagers sitting in its classrooms?

visual.credit: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beats.say: We'll keep following this story on the thirteenth, and after. If you'd like to see where it goes, subscribing to STRATA is the simplest way not to miss it.
